title: Is ‘first in family’ a good indicator for widening university participation?
summary_en: Many universities use 'first in family' (FiF) status as a target for widening-participation efforts, but is it actually picking out the disadvantaged? Adamecz-Völgyi and co-authors use nationally representative English data linked to administrative records to test the indicator's predictive power for both university entry and graduation, with parametric (logit) and non-parametric (random forest) models. They find FiF is a substantial barrier to entry and graduation, over and above other measures of disadvantage, working through the channel of early educational attainment. The indicator earns its place in widening-participation policy.
data_used: England's Next Steps longitudinal survey (the cohort followed from age 13/14) linked to the National Pupil Database administrative records on schooling and to higher-education enrolment / completion records. Models compare FiF against family-income, parental-education, and free-school-meals indicators.
policy_relevance: Speaks directly to Hungarian and EU widening-participation policy (ITM HE strategy, OFI policy briefs, EU Structural Funds equity targets): suggests Hungarian universities and the OH should formally collect first-in-family status at admission and use it as a stand-alone equity target rather than relying on parental-income measures alone. The English evidence is portable in framing, but Hungarian validation against KIR / felvi data is recommended before policy adoption.
